To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
trophic efficiency (TTE) is generally enhanced by increased variability in resource supply, but that TTE is also generally reduced with increased nutrient enrichment.

(1) trophic transfer efficiencies tend to be enhanced with increasing variability of resources, and (2) trophic efficien- cies tend to be reduced with increasing nutrient enrichment, particularly in systems subject to intense top-down control at upper tro- phic levels.

(i) the efficiency of trophic transfer from phytoplankton to zooplankton is enhanced by habitat variability, and (ii) trophic transfer effi- ciency is reduced at moderately eutropic nutrient levels, and this reduction is exacerbated by intense predation control at upper tro- phic levels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of nutrient enrichment on the efficiency of trophic transfer of primary pro- duction to growth of higher trophic levels, particularly in shallow aquatic systems.
the effects of resource variability, nutrient enrichment and trophic interactions on the efficiency with which phytoplank- ton production is transferred through food webs.
the role of nutrient enrichment in coastal ecosystems, and how this may affect the trophic efficiency of energy flow through these systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the trophic transfer effi- ciency of aquatic ecosystems is a function of the nutrient loading and the trophic level of the organism.
the trophic transfer efficiencies are generally higher in the systems with high resource variability and low nutrient concentrations.
the trophic efficiency of pelagic food webs is enhanced by habitat variability, but reduced with increased nutrient enrichment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

nutrient enrichment can be a double-edged sword in terms of trophic transfer, with the potential to enhance or diminish trophic transfer efficiencies depending on the relative strength of top-down and bottom-up control.

the efficiency with which primary production is transferred to growth at higher trophic levels is strongly influenced by both nutrient enrichment and variability of resources, but the relative importance of these effects is dependent on the specific model formulation.

nutrient enrichment can have complex effects on trophic efficiency, depending on resource variability and top-down control of upper trophic groups, but that these effects tend to be detrimental to the efficiency of resource utilization at upper trophi- c levels.
The main takeaway from our work is that
trophic efficiency may be a sensitive and useful indicator of ecosystem health.
the efficiency with which primary production is transferred to higher trophic levels is strongly dependent on the relative strength of top-down control of zooplank- ton and fish populations.
the trophic transfer efficien- cy in coastal ecosystems is likely to be strongly influenced by nutrient enrichment and habitat vari- ability.
